a: The twelve Olympian gods were the principal deities of the Greek pantheon who resided atop Mount Olympus. They included Zeus (king of the gods, god of sky and thunder), Hera (queen of the gods, goddess of marriage), Poseidon (god of the sea and earthquakes), Athena (goddess of wisdom and warfare), Apollo (god of music, prophecy, and healing), Artemis (goddess of the hunt and wilderness), Ares (god of war), Aphrodite (goddess of love and beauty), Hephaestus (god of fire and craftsmanship), Hermes (messenger god, patron of travelers), Demeter (goddess of agriculture and harvest), and Hestia (goddess of the hearth) — though Hestia sometimes yielded her seat to Dionysus. These gods ruled over every aspect of human life and the natural world, often intervening directly in mortal affairs.

a: Zeus was the supreme ruler of the Olympian gods and the god of the sky, thunder, lightning, law, order, and justice. He was the youngest son of the Titans Cronus and Rhea, whom he overthrew in the Titanomachy, a ten-year war that established the Olympian reign. Zeus was known for his many romantic affairs with both goddesses and mortal women, producing a vast array of offspring including Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Hermes, Perseus, Heracles, and Helen of Troy. His symbols included the thunderbolt, the eagle, the bull, and the oak tree, and he wielded ultimate authority over gods and mortals from his throne on Mount Olympus.

a: Heracles (known as Hercules in Roman mythology) was the greatest of the Greek heroes, a demigod son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene. Driven mad by Hera, he killed his own wife and children, and as penance was ordered to perform twelve seemingly impossible labors for King Eurystheus. These labors included slaying the Nemean Lion (whose hide became his iconic cloak), destroying the nine-headed Lernaean Hydra, capturing the Golden Hind of Artemis, retrieving the Erymanthian Boar, cleaning the Augean stables in a single day, defeating the Stymphalian Birds, capturing the Cretan Bull, stealing the man-eating Mares of Diomedes, obtaining the girdle of Hippolyta (Queen of the Amazons), capturing the cattle of the monstrous Geryon, fetching the golden apples of the Hesperides, and capturing Cerberus from the Underworld. After his death, Heracles was granted immortality and ascended to Mount Olympus as a god.

a: Greek mythology is filled with iconic creatures and monsters. Medusa was one of the three Gorgon sisters, a winged female with living venomous snakes for hair whose gaze could turn anyone to stone; she was beheaded by the hero Perseus. The Minotaur was a half-man, half-bull creature born from the union of Queen Pasiphaë and a sacred bull, imprisoned in the Labyrinth of Crete and eventually slain by Theseus. Cerberus was the three-headed hound of Hades who guarded the gates of the Underworld, ensuring the dead could not leave and the living could not enter unbidden. The Lernaean Hydra was a massive serpent-like water monster with nine heads that grew two more when cut, making it nearly invincible until Heracles cauterized each stump. Other famous creatures include the Chimera (a fire-breathing hybrid of lion, goat, and serpent), Pegasus (the winged horse), the Cyclopes (one-eyed giants), the Sirens (enchanting singers who lured sailors to their doom), and the Griffin (half-eagle, half-lion).

a: Perseus was a legendary Greek hero and the son of Zeus and the mortal Danaë, who was famously known for slaying the Gorgon Medusa. Assisted by the gods, he obtained winged sandals from Hermes, a reflective bronze shield from Athena, a helmet of invisibility from Hades, and a magical sword. Using Athena's shield as a mirror to avoid Medusa's petrifying gaze, he beheaded her while she slept, and from her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus. Perseus later used Medusa's head as a weapon to rescue the princess Andromeda from a sea monster, and after his death he was placed among the stars as a constellation.

Theseus the Athenian hero
a: Theseus was the great Athenian hero and legendary king of Athens, best known for his defeat of the Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete. He volunteered to be among the seven youths and seven maidens sent as tribute to King Minos, where he entered the Labyrinth and slew the half-man, half-bull Minotaur with his bare hands. He escaped the maze using a ball of thread given to him by Ariadne, the daughter of King Minos, which he unwound as he went in and followed back out. Theseus also unified the region of Attica under Athenian rule and was credited with founding Athenian democracy, making him a cultural symbol of Athenian identity.

a: Achilles was the greatest Greek warrior of the Trojan War and the central character of Homer's Iliad. He was the son of the mortal Peleus and the sea nymph Thetis, who dipped him in the River Styx as an infant to make him invulnerable — except for his heel by which she held him, giving rise to the term 'Achilles' heel.' Enraged when King Agamemnon took his war prize Briseis, Achilles withdrew from battle, allowing the Trojans to gain ground, until his close friend Patroclus was killed by Hector. Achilles then returned to slay Hector and dragged his body around Troy, though he eventually relented and returned it for proper burial, before being killed himself by an arrow to his heel shot by Paris.
